svg.text: You are given the top and the bottom. The gap is bridged by adding zero in a useful form.
GIVEN — where the proof starts
= lim (h→0) [ f(x+h)·g(x+h) − f(x)·g(x) ] / h
THE MOVE: add and subtract f(x)·g(x+h) in the numerator
this changes nothing — it is adding zero — but it creates two difference quotients
THE LINES TO FILL IN
= lim [ f(x+h)g(x+h) − f(x)g(x+h) + f(x)g(x+h) − f(x)g(x) ] / h
add zero
= lim { [f(x+h) − f(x)]·g(x+h) + f(x)·[g(x+h) − g(x)] } / h
group and factor
= lim [f(x+h)−f(x)]/h · lim g(x+h) + f(x) · lim [g(x+h)−g(x)]/h
split the limit
and lim (h→0) g(x+h) = g(x), because g is continuous at x
— which holds since g is differentiable there
GIVEN — the last two lines
= lim [f(x+h)−f(x)]/h · g(x) + f(x) · lim [g(x+h)−g(x)]/h
= (d/dx) f(x) · g(x) + f(x) · (d/dx) g(x)
Why subtract f(x)·g(x+h) and not something else?
It is the "mixed" term: it shares g(x+h) with the first product and f(x) with the second,
so each half of the split lands on a genuine difference quotient — one for f, one for g.
The other mixed term f(x+h)·g(x) works equally well; it just shifts the continuity appeal from g onto f.
Identity checked on 500 random quadruples; the finished rule checked numerically at several points.
